Suppose you are listening to an out-door live concert sitting at a distance of 150 m from the speakers. Your friend is listening to the live broadcast of the concert in another country and the radio signal has to travel 3000 km to reach him. Who will hear the music first and what will be the time difference between the two? Velocity of light \(= 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s and that of sound is 330 m/s.
solution:
Time taken by sound to reach you

\(= \dfrac{150}{330}\,s = 0.4546\)

Time taken by the broadcasted sound (which is done by EM waves having velocity \(= 3 \times 10^{8}\) m/s)

\(= \dfrac{3000\ \mathrm{km}}{3 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{km/s}} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{3}}{3 \times 10^{5}} = 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}\)

\(\therefore\) your friend will hear the sound first. The time difference will be

\(= 0.4546 - 0.01\)

\(= 0.4446\ \mathrm{s}\)

stem: A man shouts loudly close to a high wall. He hears an echo. If the man is at 40 m from the wall, how long after the shout will the echo be heard? (speed of sound in air = 330 m/s)
solution:
The distance travelled by the sound wave

\(= 2 \times\) distance from man to wall.

\(= 2 \times 40\)

\(= 80\ \mathrm{m}\)

\(\therefore\) Time taken to travel the distance \(= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}\)

\(= \dfrac{80\ \mathrm{m}}{330\ \mathrm{m/s}}\)

\(= 0.24\ \mathrm{s}\)

\(\therefore\) The man will hear the echo 0.24 s after he shouts.
_note: The book prints this example's solution label in LOWERCASE as "solution:" — every other example in the chapter prints "Solution:". That casing difference is the whole explanation of the chapter's 7-Example / 6-Solution-marker gap; no example is missing its solution.

stem: When heard independently, two sound waves produce sensations of 60 db and 55 db respectively. How much will the sensation be if those are sounded together, perfectly in phase?
solution:
\(L_1 = 60\,db = 10\,log_{10}\dfrac{I_1}{I_0}\quad \therefore \dfrac{I_1}{I_0} = 10^{6}\ \text{or}\ I_1 = 10^{6} I_0\)

Similarly, \(I_2 = 10^{5.5} I_0\)

As the waves combine perfectly in phase, the vector addition of their amplitudes will be given by \(A^{2} = (A_1 + A_2)^{2} = A_1^{2} + A_2^{2} + 2A_1A_2\)

As intensity is proportional to square of the amplitude.

\(\therefore I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1 I_2}\)

\(= 10^{5} I_0 \left(10^{1} + 10^{0.5} + 2\sqrt{10^{1.5}}\right)\)

\(= 10^{5} I_0 \left(10 + 3.1623 + 2 \times 10^{0.75}\right)\)

\(= 24.41 \times 10^{5} I_0 = 2.441 \times 10^{6} I_0\)

\(\therefore L = 10\,log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right) = 10\,log_{10}\left(2.441 \times 10^{6}\right)\)

\(= 10\left[log_{10}(2.441) + log_{10}\left(10^{6}\right)\right]\)

\(+ 10\,(0.3876 = 6)\)

\(= 63.876\,db \approx 64\ db\)

It is interesting to note that there is only a marginal increase in the loudness.
_note: PRINTED-SOLUTION DEFECT, transcribed verbatim, NOT repaired: the penultimate line prints "+10(0.3876 =6)" — a stray leading plus and an equals sign where a plus belongs. It must read "= 10(0.3876 + 6)", which is what gives the printed 63.876. Value and final answer are correct.

stem: A rocket is moving at a speed of 220 m/s towards a stationary target. It emits a wave of frequency 1200 Hz. Some of the sound reaching the target gets reflected back to the rocket as an echo. Calculate (1) The frequency of sound detected by the target and (2) The frequency of echo detected by rocket (velocity of sound = 330 m/s.)
solution:
Given, target stationary, i.e.,

\(\mathrm{v}_L = 0,\ \mathrm{v}_s = 220\ \mathrm{m/s},\ \mathrm{v} = 330\ \mathrm{m/s}\)

\(n_0 = 1200\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

To find the frequency of sound detected by the target we have to used Eq. (8.25)

\(n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v} - \mathrm{v}_s}\right]\)

\(n = 1200\left[\dfrac{330}{330 - 220}\right]\)

\(n = 3600\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

The frequency of sound detected by the target = 3600 Hz.

When echo is heard by rocket's detector, target is considered as source

\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_s = 0\)

The frequency of sound emitted by the source (i.e. target) is \(n_0 = 3600\) Hz, and the frequency detected by rocket is \(n'\). Now listener is approaching the source and so we have to use.

\(n' = n\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v} + \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v}}\right]\)

\(n = 3600\left[\dfrac{330 + 220}{330}\right]\)

\(n = 6000\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

The frequency of echo detected by rocket = 6000 Hz

stem:
A bat, flying at velocity \(V_B = 12.5\) m/s, is followed by a car running at velocity \(V_C = 50\) m/s. Actual directions of the velocities of the car and the bat are as shown in the figure below, both being in the same horizontal plane (the plane of the figure): the line joining the car and the bat is horizontal, the car's velocity \(V_C = 50\) m/s points forward and upward at \(53^\circ\) to that line, and the bat's velocity \(V_B = 12.5\) m/s points forward and upward at \(37^\circ\) to the same line, the bat being ahead of the car. To detect the car, the bat radiates ultrasonic waves of frequency 36 kHz. Speed of sound at surrounding temperature is 350 m/s.

There is an ultrasonic frequency detector fitted in the car. Calculate the frequency recorded by this detector.

The ultrasonic waves radiated by the bat are reflected by the car. The bat detects these waves and from the detected frequency, it knows about the speed of the car. Calculate the frequency of the reflected waves as detected by the bat. \((\sin 37^\circ = \cos 53^\circ \approx 0.6,\ \sin 53^\circ = \cos 37^\circ \approx 0.8)\)
solution:
As shown in the figure below, the components of velocities of the bat and the car, along the line joining them, are

\(V_C \cos 53^\circ \cong 50 \times 0.6 = 30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and

\(V_B \cos 37^\circ \cong 12.5 \times 0.8 = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

These should be used while calculating the doppler shifted frequencies.

Doppler shifted frequency, \(n = n_0\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{v} \pm \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v} \mp \mathrm{v}_s}\right)\); upper signs to be used during approach, lower signs during recede.

**Part I:** Frequency radiated by the bat \(n_0 = 36 \times 10^{3}\) Hz, Frequency detected by the detector in the car = \(n\) = ?

In this case, bat is the source which is moving away from the car (receding) while the detector in the car is the listener, who is approaching the source (bat). \(\mathrm{v}_s = V_B\cos 37^\circ = 10\) m/s and \(\mathrm{v}_L = V_C \cos 53^\circ = 30\) m/s

The source (bat) is receding, while the listener (car) is approaching \(\therefore n = n_0\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{v} + \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v} + \mathrm{v}_s}\right)\)

\(\therefore n = 36 \times 10^{3}\left(\dfrac{350 + 30}{350 + 10}\right)\)

\(= 38 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 38\ \mathrm{kHz}\)

**Part II:** Reflected frequency, as detected by the bat: Frequency reflected by the car is the Doppler shifted frequency as detected at the car. Thus, this time, the car is the source with emitted frequency \(n_0 = 38 \times 10^{3}\) Hz, \(n\) = ?

Car, the source, is approaching the listener (bat).

Thus, \(\mathrm{v}_S = \mathrm{v}_C\cos 53^\circ = 30\ \mathrm{m/s}\)

Thus, \(\mathrm{v}_L = \mathrm{v}_B\cos 37^\circ = 10\ \mathrm{m/s}\)

Now bat-the listener is receding while car the source is approaching \(\therefore n = n_0\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{v} - \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v} - \mathrm{v}_s}\right)\)

\(\therefore n = 38 \times 10^{3}\left(\dfrac{350 - 10}{350 - 30}\right)\)

\(= 38 \times 10^{3} \times \dfrac{34}{32}\)

\(= 40.375 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

\(= 40.375\ \mathrm{kHz}\)
diagramNote: The book prints an unnumbered vector diagram twice for this example (once with the question on p-14 and once inside the solution): a horizontal dashed line joins the car (left) and the bat (right); V_C = 50 m/s is drawn from the car at 53 degrees above that line and V_B = 12.5 m/s from the bat at 37 degrees above it, both pointing forward-and-up. The solution's copy additionally drops perpendiculars showing the components V_C cos 53 = 30 m/s and V_B cos 37 = 10 m/s along the line of sight. The stem describes the geometry in words so the question is answerable without the figure.

A certain sound wave in air has a speed 340 m/s and wavelength 1.7 m for this wave, calculate

a) the frequency

An echo-sounder in a fishing boat receives an echo from a shoal of fish 0.45 s after it was sent. If the speed of sound in water is 1500 m/s, how deep is the shoal?

A girl stands 170 m away from a high wall and claps her hands at a steady rate so that each clap coincides with the echo of the one before.

a) If she makes 60 claps in 1 minute, what value should be the speed of sound in air?

b) Now, she moves to another location and finds that she should now make 45 claps in 1 minute to coincide with successive echoes. Calculate her distance for the new position from the wall.
_note: SUSPECTED ANSWER-KEY ERROR IN PART (b), reported not repaired. Part (a) fixes the reading: 60 claps in 1 minute is a 1 s interval, and 2*170/1 = 340 m/s, which is the printed answer. On the same reading 45 claps in 1 minute is a 60/45 = 4/3 s interval, so 2d = 340*(4/3) and d = 226.67 m, not the printed 255 m. The printed 255 m requires an interval of 2*255/340 = 1.5 s, i.e. 40 claps per minute. So either the key is wrong or the stem should read 40 claps; the book's own part (a) is what makes the two irreconcilable.
